steps: Identify the shape (or split a compound shape)
Substitute the values (check you're using the perpendicular height)
Calculate and include units (cm², m², etc.)
method_card.title: How to Find Area & Perimeter
method_card.content:
Key area formulas:

$$\text{Rectangle} = l \times w \qquad \text{Triangle} = \frac{1}{2} \times b \times h \qquad \text{Parallelogram} = b \times h$$

$$\text{Trapezium} = \frac{1}{2}(a + b) \times h \qquad \text{Circle} = \pi r^2 \qquad \text{Circumference} = 2\pi r = \pi d$$

For compound shapes, split into simpler shapes and add (or subtract) their areas. Always use the perpendicular height, not the slant height.
method_card.example:
Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm and height 4 cm.

\(A = \frac{1}{2}(6 + 10) \times 4 = \frac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 4 = 32\) cm²

gold.display: A running track is two straight sides of 100 m and two semicircular ends of diameter 60 m. Find the total perimeter to the nearest metre.
gold.hint: Two straights plus one full circle; add before rounding.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you used 30 instead of the diameter 60 for the circular part. The two ends make one full circle: π × 60 ≈ 188.5, plus the two 100 m straights, giving about 388 m.
misconceptions.note: Student uses radius (30) instead of diameter (60): pi x 30 = 94.2, total 200 + 94 = 294 m.

guided_steps.say: The perimeter is the two straight sides plus the two curved ends. The two semicircular ends together make one full circle of diameter 60 m.

guided_steps.pre: The two ends make one full circle, circumference π × diameter. On your calculator, π × 60 =
guided_steps.hint: Type 60 × π. It is 188.5 to 1 d.p.

guided_steps.pre: Add, using the calculator's full value (not the rounded 188.5), then round the total to the nearest metre: 200 + π × 60 =
guided_steps.hint: Type 200 + 60 × π. It gives 388.49..., which rounds down to 388.

guided_steps.pre: Check the straights alone come to 200: 100 + 100 =
guided_steps.done: The straights give 200 m and the circle adds about 188.5 m, total 388 m. Rounding the 188.5 too early would have given 389, the classic slip.

gold.display: A sector has radius 8 cm and angle \(135°\). Find the area to 1 d.p.
gold.hint: Angle over 360 times π r squared.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you used 135 out of 180 instead of out of 360. A sector is angle over 360: (135 ÷ 360) × π × 8² ≈ 75.4 cm².
misconceptions.note: Student uses 135/180 instead of 135/360: 0.75 x 64pi = 150.8.

guided_steps.say: A sector is a fraction of a whole circle. The fraction is the angle over 360.

guided_steps.pre: Multiply the fraction, the square and π, then round to 1 d.p.: 0.375 × 64 × π =

guided_steps.done: That returns the angle, 135°, so the fraction was right and the area is 75.4 cm².

gold.display: A circle has area \(200\) cm². Find the circumference to 1 d.p.
gold.hint: Turn the area into a radius, then find the circumference.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you skipped the square root. From area = π r², first r² = 200 ÷ π, then r = √(200 ÷ π) ≈ 7.98, so C = 2πr ≈ 50.1 cm.
misconceptions.note: Student skips sqrt: treats r = 200/pi = 63.66, C = 2pi x 63.66 = 400.

guided_steps.say: Two stages: turn the area back into a radius, then use the radius to find the circumference.

guided_steps.pre: Divide the area by π: 200 ÷ π =
That is the radius squared. Square-root it: √63.66 =
Now the circumference: 2 × π × 7.98, to 1 d.p. =
Check by squaring the radius and using π: 7.98² × π ≈
guided_steps.done: That returns the area, about 200 cm², so the circumference 50.1 cm is right.

gold.display: A sector has arc length 12 cm and radius 9 cm. Find the sector angle to the nearest degree.
gold.hint: Arc over full circumference gives the fraction; times 360 for the angle.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you left the 2 out of the circumference. Arc = (θ ÷ 360) × 2πr, so θ = 12 × 360 ÷ (2 × π × 9) ≈ 76°.
misconceptions.note: Student omits the 2: uses arc = (theta/360) x pi r, giving 153.

guided_steps.say: Arc length is a fraction of the full circumference. The fraction is the angle over 360, so work backwards to the angle.

guided_steps.pre: The arc is 12 out of that whole circumference. Fraction of the circle: 12 ÷ 56.55 =
Multiply the fraction by 360 for the angle, to the nearest degree: 0.2122 × 360 =

guided_steps.hint: Should give the arc length back, 12.
guided_steps.done: That returns the arc length, 12 cm, so the angle 76° is right.

gold.display: An annulus (ring) has outer radius 10 cm and inner radius 6 cm. Find the area to 1 d.p.
gold.hint: Square both radii, subtract, then times π.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you subtracted the radii before squaring. Square each first: π × (10² − 6²) = π × 64 ≈ 201.1 cm².
misconceptions.note: Student subtracts radii first: pi(10-6)^2 = pi x 16 = 50.3.

guided_steps.say: An annulus is a big circle with a smaller circle cut out. Find each area, then subtract. Square each radius BEFORE subtracting.

guided_steps.pre: Subtract the squares, then multiply by π, to 1 d.p.: (100 − 36) × π = 64 × π =

guided_steps.done: 64 × π ≈ 201.1, and subtracting the squares (not the radii) is the key move, so 201.1 cm² is right.

bronze.display: Find the area of a rectangle with length 9 cm and width 5 cm.
bronze.hint: Multiply length by width; do not add the sides.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you found the perimeter, 2 × (9 + 5) = 28 cm. Area is different: multiply the sides, 9 × 5 = 45 cm².
misconceptions.note: Student uses perimeter 2(9+5)=28 instead of area.

guided_steps.say: Area of a rectangle is length × width. Just multiply the two sides, nothing else.

guided_steps.hint: The width, straight from the question.
It should give the width you started with.
guided_steps.done: That returns the width, 5 cm, so 45 cm² is right.

bronze.display: Find the perimeter of a rectangle with length 12 cm and width 7 cm.
bronze.hint: Add a length and a width, then double.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you added just one length and one width. A rectangle has two of each, so double it: 2 × (12 + 7) = 38 cm.
misconceptions.note: Student adds one length and one width (12+7=19) without doubling.

guided_steps.say: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. For a rectangle, add a length and a width, then double.

guided_steps.pre: First add one length and one width: 12 + 7 =
guided_steps.hint: Just add the two given sides.

guided_steps.pre: Now double it, because there are two lengths and two widths: 19 × 2 =
Check by adding all four sides: 12 + 7 + 12 + 7 =
guided_steps.done: Same answer, so 38 cm is right.

bronze.display: Find the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm.

misconceptions.message: That is base × height. A triangle is only half of that, so halve it: ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm².
misconceptions.note: Student omits the half: 10x6=60.

guided_steps.say: Area of a triangle is half of base × height.

guided_steps.pre: Now halve it, because a triangle is half a rectangle: 60 ÷ 2 =

guided_steps.done: That returns base × height (60), so 30 cm² is right.

bronze.display: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 8 cm and height 5 cm.
bronze.hint: Base times height, and do not halve (it is not a triangle).

misconceptions.message: It looks like you halved, as for a triangle. A parallelogram is not halved: area = base × height = 8 × 5 = 40 cm².
misconceptions.note: Student applies triangle half: 1/2 x 8 x 5 = 20.

guided_steps.say: Area of a parallelogram is base × perpendicular height. No halving, unlike a triangle.

guided_steps.hint: The height, straight from the question.

guided_steps.done: That returns the height, 5 cm, so 40 cm² is right.

bronze.display: Find the circumference of a circle with diameter 14 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.
bronze.hint: Circumference is π times the diameter; the diameter is already given.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you used the radius (half of 14). Circumference uses the whole diameter: π × 14 ≈ 44.0 cm.
misconceptions.note: Student uses radius 7 instead of diameter 14: pi x 7 = 22.0.

guided_steps.say: Circumference is π × diameter. The diameter is given, so there is no halving here.

guided_steps.pre: Multiply the diameter by π: 14 × π =
Round to 1 decimal place: 43.98 rounds to
guided_steps.hint: The second decimal is 8, so the first decimal rounds up.

guided_steps.pre: Sense check: the circumference is a bit over 3 diameters, and 3 × 14 =
guided_steps.done: 44.0 is just above 42, exactly what π (a little over 3) gives, so it is right.

bronze.display: Find the area of a circle with radius 5 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.
bronze.hint: Square the radius first, then multiply by π.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you multiplied π by the radius. Area needs the radius squared: π × 5² = π × 25 ≈ 78.5 cm².
misconceptions.note: Student forgets to square: pi x 5 = 15.7.

guided_steps.say: Area of a circle is π × radius². Square the radius first, then multiply by π.

guided_steps.pre: Now multiply by π and round to 1 d.p.: 25 × π =
Sense check: without π it would be 25, and π is a bit over 3, so 3 × 25 =
guided_steps.done: The real area uses π, so it is just over 75: 78.5 cm² fits.

bronze.display: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 5 cm and 9 cm and height 6 cm.
bronze.hint: Add the parallel sides, times the height, then halve.

misconceptions.message: That is (sum of parallel sides) × height. The trapezium formula halves it: ½ × (5 + 9) × 6 = 42 cm².
misconceptions.note: Student omits the half: (5+9)x6 = 84.

guided_steps.say: Area of a trapezium is half of (the two parallel sides added) × height.

guided_steps.done: That returns (sum of sides) × height, so 42 cm² is right.

bronze.display: A square has perimeter 48 cm. Find its area.
bronze.hint: Divide the perimeter by 4 for the side, then square it.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you gave the perimeter as the area. First find one side, 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm, then square it: 12² = 144 cm².
misconceptions.note: Student reports perimeter 48 as the area.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you squared the whole perimeter. Find one side first, 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm, then square that: 12² = 144 cm².
misconceptions.note: Student squares the perimeter: 48^2 = 2304.

guided_steps.say: Two steps. A square has four equal sides, so first find one side, then square it for the area.

guided_steps.pre: Now the area: square the side, 12² = 12 × 12 =

guided_steps.done: That returns the side, 12 cm, so 144 cm² is right.

silver.display: Find the area of a circle with diameter 18 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.
silver.hint: Halve the diameter to get the radius before using π r squared.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you used the diameter (18) as the radius. Halve it first: r = 9, then A = π × 9² ≈ 254.5 cm².
misconceptions.note: Student uses diameter as radius: pi x 18^2 = 1017.9.

guided_steps.say: The diameter is given, but the area formula needs the radius. Halve the diameter first.

guided_steps.pre: Multiply by π and round to 1 d.p.: 81 × π =
Check the radius came from the diameter: 9 × 2 =
guided_steps.done: That returns the diameter, 18 cm, so using r = 9 was right and the area is 254.5 cm².

silver.display: A circle has circumference 31.4 cm. Find the radius to 1 d.p. (Use \(\pi = 3.14\))
silver.hint: Divide the circumference by 2π to get the radius.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you divided by π only, which gives the diameter. The radius needs dividing by 2π: 31.4 ÷ 6.28 = 5.0 cm.
misconceptions.note: Student divides by pi only: 31.4/3.14 = 10 (diameter).

guided_steps.say: Circumference is 2 × π × radius. Here the circumference is known, so work backwards to the radius.

guided_steps.done: That returns the circumference, so the radius is 5.0 cm.

silver.display: An L-shaped room can be split into a rectangle measuring 8 m by 4 m and another rectangle measuring 3 m by 5 m. Find the total floor area.
silver.hint: Find each rectangle's area, then add them.

misconceptions.message: Split the L into two rectangles: 8 × 4 = 32 and 3 × 5 = 15. Add them: 32 + 15 = 47 m².
misconceptions.note: Compound addition has no single determinate wrong answer, so expect is null.

guided_steps.say: Split the L into two rectangles, find each area, then add.

guided_steps.done: That returns the first rectangle's area, so 47 m² is right.

silver.display: Find the area of a quarter circle with radius 10 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.
silver.hint: Find the full circle area, then take a quarter.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you found the whole circle. This is a quarter, so divide by 4: (π × 10²) ÷ 4 ≈ 78.5 cm².
misconceptions.note: Student uses full circle: pi x 100 = 314.2.

guided_steps.say: A quarter circle is one quarter of a full circle. Take the quarter before the π so the numbers stay tidy.

guided_steps.pre: Multiply by π and round to 1 d.p.: 25 × π =
Check by scaling back to a full circle: 78.5 × 4 =
guided_steps.done: That is π × 100, the whole circle (≈ 314), so the quarter 78.5 cm² is right.

silver.display: A trapezium has area 60 cm², parallel sides 8 cm and 12 cm. Find the height.
silver.hint: Halve the sum of the parallel sides, then divide the area by that.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you left out the half. The formula is area = ½ × (8 + 12) × h, so 60 = 10h and h = 6 cm.
misconceptions.note: Student omits half when rearranging: 60/(8+12) = 3.

guided_steps.say: Use the trapezium formula backwards. Area = half × (sum of parallel sides) × height, and the height is missing.

guided_steps.pre: So area = 10 × height. Divide to find the height: 60 ÷ 10 =

guided_steps.done: That returns the area, 60 cm², so the height is 6 cm.

silver.display: Find the perimeter of a semicircle with radius 7 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.
silver.hint: Add the curved half-circumference to the straight diameter.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you found only the curved edge (π × 7 ≈ 22.0). A semicircle's perimeter also includes the straight diameter, 14 cm: total ≈ 36.0 cm.
misconceptions.note: Student forgets the diameter: only pi r = 22.0.

guided_steps.say: A semicircle's perimeter is the curved half PLUS the straight diameter across the middle. Both parts matter.

guided_steps.pre: The straight edge is the diameter: 2 × 7 =
The curved edge is half the circumference: π × 7, to 1 d.p. =

guided_steps.hint: Add the straight and curved parts.

guided_steps.pre: Check the straight edge: half of the diameter, 14 ÷ 2 =
guided_steps.done: That returns the radius, 7 cm, so the perimeter 36.0 cm is right.

silver.display: The area of a circle is 50.3 cm². Find the radius to 1 d.p.
silver.hint: Divide the area by π, then square-root to get the radius.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you stopped at the radius squared. Take the square root: r = √(50.3 ÷ π) ≈ √16 = 4.0 cm.
misconceptions.note: Student stops at r^2 = 16 and does not square-root.

guided_steps.say: Area is π × radius². The area is known, so undo it: divide by π, then square-root.

guided_steps.pre: Divide the area by π: 50.3 ÷ π =
That is the radius squared. Square-root it: √16 =
Check by working forwards: 4² × π = 16 × π =
guided_steps.done: That returns the area, 50.3 cm², so the radius is 4.0 cm.

problem_bank.bronze_description: Put the numbers straight into one standard area or perimeter formula.
problem_bank.silver_description: One extra step first: halve a diameter, take a fraction of a circle, rearrange to find a missing length, or add two shapes.
problem_bank.gold_description: Chain several steps, often with sectors, rings, or a mix of perimeter and area.

worked_examples.question: Find the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and height 8 cm.
Find the area of a circle with radius 7 cm. Give your answer to 1 d.p.
A semicircle has diameter 10 cm. Find its perimeter to 1 d.p.

bronze.title: Bronze: one formula, straight in
steps: Pick the shape and its formula. Rectangle area is \(l \times w\); triangle is \(\tfrac{1}{2}bh\); parallelogram is \(b \times h\); trapezium is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b)h\).
Put the numbers straight in and calculate. Do not muddle area with perimeter: area multiplies (units cm²); perimeter adds the sides (units cm).
For circles, circumference is \(\pi d\) and area is \(\pi r^2\). Square the radius before multiplying by \(\pi\).

example.question: Find the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and height 8 cm.

silver.title: Silver: one step first, then the formula
steps: The formula will not take the numbers as given, so do one preparation step first.
Common preparations: halve a diameter to get the radius; take a fraction of a circle (half, quarter); rearrange a formula to find a missing length; or split a compound shape into rectangles and add.
Then finish as in bronze, and check by working back to a number you were given.

example.question: Find the area of a circle with diameter 18 cm (1 d.p.).

steps.label: Check
steps.content: Double the radius: \(9 \times 2 = 18\) cm, the given diameter. ✓

gold.title: Gold: several steps chained
steps: Gold questions combine steps, often with sectors, rings, or a mix of straight and curved edges.
Work in stages and keep full accuracy on your calculator until the very end. Rounding partway (say a circle's circumference) can push the final answer out by a whole unit.
A sector or arc is a fraction \(\tfrac{\theta}{360}\) of the whole circle; a ring is the big area minus the small area (square each radius first).

example.question: A sector has radius 8 cm and angle 135°. Find the area (1 d.p.).

opener.label: Before any formulas
opener.display:
A kitchen floor tiled 4 squares across and 3 squares up:
▦▦▦▦
▦▦▦▦
▦▦▦▦

steps.say: No formulas yet. Just count the tiles on this floor.
steps.hint: 4 tiles in each row, 3 rows. Count them, or do 4 × 3.

steps.say: Counting those tiles IS finding the area: four in a row, three rows, 4 × 3 = 12. Area of a rectangle is just length × width.
steps.pre: Now the border. Going all the way round the edge, count the tile-sides: top 4, right 3, bottom 4, left 3, added together =

steps.say: That trip round the edge is the perimeter: add every side, 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 14, the same as 2 × (4 + 3). Area fills the inside (multiply); perimeter goes round the edge (add). Those two ideas run through every question here. Algebra just calls the sides \(l\) and \(w\): area \(= l \times w\), perimeter \(= 2(l + w)\).

bronze.label: Together: your first one

steps.say: Bronze means the numbers go straight into a formula. Trapezium area is half of (the parallel sides added) × height.
